title: Enhancing data usability and market visibility under new regulatory changes
text:
Enhancing data usability and market visibility under new regulatory changes
Europe’s transparency reforms promised consolidation; instead, they are delivering choice. As the UK (FCA) and EU (ESMA) shorten deferral periods and two different bond CTPs (Consolidated Tape Providers) enter the market at different times, firms are navigating a more complex landscape of transparency data — where usability, not availability, is the real differentiator.
The question is no longer whether data is available, but whether it can be trusted enough and used to make good trading decisions.
Why this matters now
Recent FCA and ESMA transparency reforms have increased the real-time publication of corporate bond prices to an estimated 80–90% of all transactions, up from around 30% previously, according to MarketAxess TraX®, our executed global fixed income data. While this marks a significant step forward for market transparency, several structural challenges remain.

- Deferral frameworks are complex.
The two regimes apply different deferral frameworks, resulting in 68 distinct deferral scenarios across corporate and sovereign bonds. That number will increase from 4th May, when ESMA’s supplementary sovereign bond deferrals come into force, adding additional volume‑masking rules for liquid sovereign instruments. Our analysis suggests that around 15% of investment-grade corporate bond volume will still be subject to the longest deferral in reporting — three months under FCA rules and four weeks under ESMA.
This means the timing of trade publication will vary materially depending on the reporting regime, trade size, and instrument— adding complexity for firms attempting to interpret transparency data across both regimes.

- Deferred volumes hide meaningful volume.
The practical impact of these deferrals became clear when the FCA transparency regime changes took effect in December 2025. While APA’s (Approved Publication Arrangements) delayed publication of approximately 75% of volumes, TraX captured the underlying trades in real time, allowing us to quantify exactly how much market activity was missing from the public view.

Impacts of the FCA deferral regime
By the close of trading each day during the first week of December 2025, TraX revealed approximately €80bn of clean, visible investment-grade corporate bond volume — compared with an estimated €32bn that would have been observable through combined FCA and ESMA public reporting alone.
Total clean volume published in Corp-IG at deferral period

TraX was able to reveal volumes much closer to true market size, delivered via our curated TraX Volume service. TraX Volume aggregates trading data from a network of more than 50 dealers and clients, applying carefully agreed size thresholds and caps to balance transparency with market protection. Participants contribute their data as subscribers to our services, and in exchange for access to TraX and our market data products.

- Data usability
Alongside completeness, usability and reliability of pricing remain key concerns. Our analysis from July 2025 – see here, shows that nearly 40% of published trades from the top 10 APAs are not immediately usable, most commonly due to duplication, and require additional processing.

Percentage of clean trades in the top 10 APAs†

†Output from TraX proprietary data-cleansing algorithms on trade data published by the top 10 APAs, covering all fixed income market activity in Q1 2025.

For firms, this means transparency often comes with a hidden cost: cleansing and normalising data before it can support accurate pricing, liquidity assessment, trading decisions, or analysis.

A different way to approach transparency
Transparency is not just a question of how much data is published, but whether that data presents a clear, clean and representative picture of market activity.
If you can consolidate data early, de-duplicate it at source, and enrich it with context, you can deliver a more usable “tape” than stitching together raw public outputs.

Introducing: TraX Tape
TraX Tape is designed to be a single, consolidated data feed that provides a clean, standardised view of all global bond market activity.
The aim is simple: provide decision-grade data so trading desks can interpret true market activity faster, with less internal data processing, and with more context than raw inputs alone can provide.
It applies UK and EU transparency rules to TraX, supplemented by additional real-time transparency for small and medium-sized trades, as agreed following consultation with our contributor community. Trades are processed through our proprietary cleansing algorithm, refined for over 20 years, and enriched with proprietary insights — including trade direction and our award-winning pricing engine CP+™.
That means clients can see whether moves are being driven by client buying, client selling, or inter-dealer activity, and assess pricing and execution quality with a far richer context than a plain trade print. The result is a more complete and reliable representation of market activity than standalone APA feeds, or future CTP outputs, can provide on their own — without forcing firms to build and maintain the same cleansing and normalisation stack internally.
How it will work

Why TraX Tape is different

- Directional clarity: client-buy, client-sell and inter-dealer indicators on every trade print, making it easier to distinguish genuine market momentum from noise.

- Cleaner data: a holistic view of all trading activity enables superior de-duplication and cleansing, reducing the hidden cost of reconciling, normalising, and validating fragmented public outputs.

- Broader coverage: In January 2026, TraX captured and published 233,342 unique trades that would not have been published under ESMA or FCA transparency regimes, driven by unique contributions from global EM markets and non-European activity — helping firms build a more representative picture of true market liquidity and flow.

- Earlier volume insight: aggregated volumes are available by end of day, ahead of public deferrals sourced from our contributor community and trading platform — so analysis is driven by what traded today, not what becomes visible weeks or months later.

- Calcs: bond-level analytics applied to each trade, including yield and spread calculations supporting faster relative-value analysis and more consistent downstream analytics.

- One connection: one consolidated connection providing access to all underlying data sources lowering operational complexity versus stitching together multiple feeds.

What this enables

- Clear directional market sentiment in real time — so teams can see what’s actually driving moves.

- Faster, more consistent price and liquidity context on each print via CP+ and analytics — supporting TCA-style insights into execution quality.

- Earlier access to meaningful market activity than public deferrals alone allow — reducing reliance on delayed, stale tape data.

- Outsourced data cleaning and consolidation — removing operational complexity and freeing teams to focus on decisioning and strategy.

TraX data In action
The market reaction to US intervention in Venezuela illustrates the value of enriched transparency. Using TraX data, clients were able to see trade direction on every transaction — insight that is not available under either the FCA or ESMA regimes. In the 5-year Venezuelan government bond (VENZ 11.950 8/5/31), client sell-offs on Monday afternoon were followed by renewed buying on Tuesday, closely mirroring sharp price movements as the news unfolded.
In addition, TraX captured activity that never became publicly visible, with 17% of Venezuelan bond trades unique to TraX in the week following the intervention. Crucially, this data was cleaned and de-duplicated in real time, allowing users to observe true market behaviour as it happened, rather than reconstruct it after the fact.
How the market reacted to the 2026 US intervention in Venezuela

What comes next
TraX Tape1 is currently being tested with our largest clients and contributors, reflecting our long-standing approach of building products in close partnership with the market. The roadmap is clear: delivery via CSV and API, followed by a graphical interface shortly thereafter. But this is just the starting point: because TraX Tape is built on proprietary data and analytics, we can continue to enhance fields, calculations, and datasets on a commercial cadence as client needs evolve.
Our ambition is to evolve TraX Tape into a truly global data source by incorporating public CTP data1 and US data sources to deliver a consistent, enriched single view of market activity across all regions. In parallel, we expect to make longer-run historical time series available, enabling back-testing and more advanced quantitative research against a dataset that extends beyond what new public tapes can offer. As firms seek usable transparency now, rather than fragmented data or uncertain future solutions, we continue to work closely with clients to help shape the next phase of transparency.
The direction of travel: an enriched public bond tape
The EU & the UK are moving towards public consolidated bond tapes — but experience from the US shows the end state is rarely “raw tape only”. Since the introduction of TRACE, the most sophisticated firms have increasingly relied on enriched TRACE products to improve usability, provide better context, and reduce internal processing.
The same landscape is emerging in Europe: two baseline public bond tapes, and a growing requirement for consolidated, cleaned, and enriched data that trading desks can actually use. TraX Tape is built for that end state — delivering the benefits of consolidation while adding the quality, coverage, and context that institutions need. We have used this model with TraX for over 20 years: with contributor-led inputs, designed around market needs, and continuously refined as usage patterns evolve.

1Our intent is to include CTP data from both the EU and UK CTPs; however, this is subject to the final terms and conditions imposed by each CTP.

title: From macro signals to execution edge in fixed income
text:
From macro signals to execution edge in fixed income
For much of the last decade, fixed income investors operated in a market environment heavily influenced by central bank policy, quantitative easing, and clear forward guidance. Today, that backdrop has shifted materially. While inflation has moderated from its peaks, real yields remain elevated, financial conditions are still relatively tight, and growth outcomes are diverging across regions. At the same time, fiscal deficits, increased bond issuance, and a more data-dependent policy framework are creating a more complex and less predictable investment landscape. These changes are prompting investors to rethink how they build portfolios and manage risk. Rather than positioning around a single macro outcome, market participants are increasingly focused on creating resilient portfolios capable of navigating a wider range of economic scenarios.
In the recent 2026 Global Fixed Income & FinTech Institutional Leaders Summit on 25 June, MarketAxess, together with senior panelists from across various financial institutions offered insights on how to navigate the current fixed income landscape. Roheet Shah, Head of Dealer Sales, APAC and Head of Hong Kong, explored the macro forces reshaping bond markets, while Cathy Cai, China Business Lead, examined how technology and market structure are helping institutions remain agile in an increasingly complex trading environment.
Navigating a macro-led structural reset for fixed income
Even as inflation eases, real yields remain structurally elevated, indicating a tight financial condition. The new Fed leadership adds another layer of complexity by turning away from forward-looking guidance toward greater reliance on data. This points to a market where liquidity is more fragmented and timing matters more.
Simultaneously, bond markets are shifting from a monetary-dominated regime to one driven by fiscal deficits and heavy issuance, particularly at the long end. The debate is whether term premium is resetting structurally higher or remains cyclical and likely to compress once issuance stabilises. Either way, fiscal and supply dynamics now compete directly with monetary signals for influence over where yields settle.
This backdrop raises a consequential question for Asia. Can the region meaningfully decouple from the US rate cycle? Historically, the US has anchored global rates through its economy, yield curve, and the dollar. This cycle shows more visible divergence, but a hawkish US path or a stronger dollar could still dominate outcomes. Decoupling is conditional rather than guaranteed, depending on how much domestic factors can take over from the US cycle.
In the centre of the picture sits China. Instead of a growth engine, the country serves as an anchor with broadly stable growth, measured policy support, even as the recovery stays uneven and questions persist around domestic demand transmission. However, investors remain cautious about whether China is moving to a genuine reflation or settling into a more stable and lower growth environment.

 “The macroeconomic context holds paramount importance for fixed income markets in the current era. Not only does it influence yields, but it also shapes market dynamics in a liquidity-constrained environment where timing has become a critical factor. Such change emphasises the importance of electronic trading platforms such as MarketAxess, which can help clients access broader liquidity, improve execution efficiency, and make better trading decisions with sufficient data while managing risk in a more complex market landscape.”

 Roheet Shah
Head of Dealer Sales, APAC & Head of Hong Kong

A consistent evolution of institutional resilience through technology and execution
The fixed income industry is entering a new phase of evolution. Today, the focus has expanded from electronification to liquidity access, data intelligence, workflow integration, and increasingly, artificial intelligence. Future competitive advantage will not only come from any single tool or technology, but an institution's ability to combine trading, data, AI, and investment processes into a unified decision-making framework.
Execution quality is increasingly becoming a source of alpha. As liquidity fragments across protocols, venues, and counterparties, execution desks are no longer operating just as an execution function. With the rise of anonymous trading, portfolio trading, automated execution, and alternative liquidity pools, these solutions have fundamentally changed how investors interact with the market. The strongest trading teams with an edge are those overseeing the workflow – from executing orders, uncovering opportunities, managing liquidity risks, and working closely with portfolio managers to improve trading outcomes. If the last decade was defined by electronification, the next is being shaped by data, where it now provides an edge to users to make better investment decisions. Liquidity forecasting, credit intelligence, relative value identification, and portfolio-level analytics are some of the key areas where data value-adds. With the improvement of market transparency, firms that will emerge as winners are those with a stronger analytical framework and decision-support capabilities, rather than those simply accumulating larger datasets.
While enthusiasm around AI remains strong, especially in relation to improving productivity in workflows, many organizations are first using AI to help with information processing, increasing investment research and operational efficiency. But its impact on actual investment decision-making remains gradual. Decision makers emphasized that successful AI adoption is not just a technology challenge – data governance, explainability, validation frameworks, risk management, and organizational readiness are also key determinants of success. To arm fixed income professionals with the research so that they can work more efficiently, MarketAxess has partnered with AIQ Markets to enable users to search bond data, compare relative value, and construct portfolios through natural language. By providing auditable answers with transparent sourcing and governance controls through AIQ Insight™, MarketAxess will pilot an exclusive version of its new tool that leverages proprietary data feeds such as CP+™ pricing information and Tradability scores.
Beyond AI, the convergence of primary, grey, and secondary markets is also essential in tackling fragmentation challenges. The partnership between MarketAxess and DirectBooks is helping bridge the gap between primary issuance, grey-market activity, and secondary trading. Shared clients can view new issue announcements, submit interest, and receive allocations in a streamlined and seamless workflow. This reflects a broader industry shift toward managing investment opportunities holistically rather than as separate stages of the investment process.
The defining edge
Portfolio resilience means letting go of an outdated rate paradigm, recognising Asia's growing independence, and building genuine cross-border flexibility. Institutional resilience means execution sophistication, robust data infrastructure, carefully governed AI, and connectivity across the bond lifecycle.
In a market where market conditions are tighter, liquidity is more fragmented, and timing matters more, resilience is no longer about avoiding disruption. It is about having the regional awareness to see where the market is heading, and the institutional capability to act on it faster than the market changes.
MarketAxess’ data, AI capabilities, and its integrated access to primary, grey and secondary markets, is the defining edge that enables traders the ability to stay competitive amidst the rapidly changing macroeconomic landscape.

title: Malaysia's MYR bond market gains momentum as institutional liquidity expands on MarketAxess
text:
Malaysia's MYR bond market gains momentum as institutional liquidity expands on MarketAxess
MarketAxess trading activity highlights the Malaysian ringgit (MYR) as one of the fastest-growing emerging market local currency bond markets on the platform in 2026, with participation accelerating across a broad range of offshore investors. The resulting mix of long-term investors, macro funds and dealers has created a diverse institutional trading ecosystem, supporting more consistent two-way trading and reinforcing Malaysia's increasingly prominent role within Asian local currency fixed income. 
Malaysia's local currency bond market is emerging as one of the more interesting success stories in Asia's fixed income landscape. As global investors continue to search for liquid, investable local currency markets offering both yield and stability, Malaysia has increasingly found its way onto the radar of both real money and hedge fund accounts. 
The backdrop has been constructive. Strong external fundamentals, including resilient external balances, a widening trade surplus and continued current account strength, have reinforced investor confidence in Malaysian assets. At the same time, Bank Negara Malaysia's decision to maintain its policy rate at 2.75% has provided investors with a stable monetary policy framework, while foreign demand for Malaysian Government Securities (MGS) has remained resilient despite ongoing uncertainty surrounding US rates, China's growth outlook and broader geopolitical developments. 
What is particularly notable is the breadth of offshore participation on MarketAxess. Flows have been driven by both real money and hedge fund investors, creating a healthy balance between long-term allocation flows and active relative value trading. 
Asset managers, insurers and pension funds have continued deploying capital into MGS and GII markets to capture attractive carry and benefit from Malaysia's stable macroeconomic backdrop. At the same time, macro and relative value hedge funds have increasingly used MYR markets to express views on BNM policy, Federal Reserve expectations, USD/MYR direction and relative value opportunities versus other Asian local markets such as Indonesia, Korea and Thailand.

MarketAxess: MGS B/S skews

Malaysia is attracting diverse investor flows 
Interestingly, trading activity on MarketAxess suggests investors remain constructive on Malaysia, but not aggressively bullish. 
MarketAxess flow data shows positioning has remained relatively balanced across much of the curve throughout 2026, even during periods of elevated global volatility. 
The clearest trend has emerged in the short end of the curve. The sub-two-year sector has generally been more heavily offered than other parts of the curve in recent months, suggesting investors have become increasingly selective about front-end exposure as expectations for meaningful near-term rate cuts have perhaps diminished. 
Rather than reflecting a more cautious view on Malaysia, the trend appears consistent with a market that broadly expects BNM to remain on hold. With domestic growth holding up well and inflation remaining relatively contained, investors may see less upside in short-dated bonds and are increasingly looking elsewhere along the curve for opportunities. 
Beyond the front end, however, the picture remains considerably more balanced. 
The 2-7 year sector has been one of the most stable areas of the MYR curve, with buy and sell skews remaining tightly range-bound throughout the year. This suggests investors remain comfortable holding intermediate-duration exposure while avoiding large directional bets. 
That dynamic aligns closely with the broader macro backdrop. Malaysia's strong external position, resilient currency and attractive carry profile continue to provide support for local fixed income assets, while the diversity of participants on MarketAxess has contributed to consistent liquidity across the intermediate sector, helping prevent the kind of broad-based selling seen in some other emerging markets. 
The 7-10 year segment exhibits a similar pattern. Flows have oscillated between modest buying and selling, but without establishing a sustained directional trend. This type of activity is typically indicative of active two-way participation from both real money and hedge fund accounts, with investors expressing relative value views and portfolio allocation decisions rather than outright duration calls. 
Growing foreign participation supports the market 
One of the defining themes this year has been the continued presence of offshore investors. 
Malaysia offers a combination that many global investors find increasingly attractive: a relatively stable currency, positive carry, resilient economic fundamentals and a central bank that has maintained a predictable policy framework. 
Those characteristics have helped support demand for MGS across a range of investor types, contributing to a more active institutional trading ecosystem on the MarketAxess platform and to Malaysia's growing relevance within regional fixed income portfolios. 
Importantly, this support is not being driven by a single investor segment or macro theme. Instead, participation has been broad-based, spanning long-only investors seeking yield opportunities as well as macro funds pursuing relative value and cross-market trades. As participation has expanded, clients have benefited from a broader range of counterparties and active price discovery. 
That diversity of participation is often a hallmark of markets that are becoming more structurally important within global investment portfolios. 
Selective rather than aggressive duration extension 
Perhaps just as important is what investors are not doing. 
Despite supportive fundamentals, there has been limited evidence of aggressive extension into the long end of the curve. Activity in the 10-20 year, 20-30 year and ultra-long sectors has generally remained muted, suggesting investors continue to approach duration exposure with a degree of caution. 
That caution is understandable. Global investors continue to navigate uncertainty around the path of US interest rates, China's growth trajectory, tariff developments and ongoing geopolitical risks. Against that backdrop, many appear comfortable maintaining exposure to Malaysia while remaining selective about extending too far out the curve. 
The result is a market that appears healthy and balanced rather than crowded or one-sided. 
Why Malaysia matters 
Taken together, the flow data reinforces a broader narrative that is developing across Asian fixed income markets. 
Malaysia is increasingly being viewed as a market that combines stability, liquidity and attractive investment opportunities. A stronger ringgit, resilient external balances, stable monetary policy and sustained foreign participation have created conditions that continue to attract global investors. 
That evolution is reflected on MarketAxess. MYR has become one of the platform's fastest-growing emerging market local currency bond markets, supported by participation from asset managers, hedge funds, banks and other institutional investors. As participation has expanded, the institutional trading ecosystem on MarketAxess has deepened, supporting broader counterparty access, more consistent two-way markets, and active price discovery across the curve.

title: More block trades are going electronic
text:
More block trades are going electronic
For years, the narrative around fixed income electronification focused on smaller, more liquid trades—the efficiency-easy wins. Block trades (for example, trades in IG Credit over $5 million) were treated as structurally different and were thought to be too impactful, too sensitive, and too reliant on relationships and balance sheets to move onto screens. But the data is beginning to tell a different story.
In Q1 2026, electronic block trading on our platform reached record average daily volume of $6.6 billion, up 35% year-on-year. That growth was broad-based: US credit block ADV rose 27%, emerging markets 47%, and Eurobonds 45%. In January alone, block ADV was up 56% year-on-year, with EM blocks growing 92% and Eurobond blocks 89%.

Q1 Electronic block trading ADV rose 35% YoY*

 +27%
 +47%
 +45%

 US credit block
 EM credit block
 Eurobonds

*The data reflects a structural shift in how large trades are initiated, priced and executed across credit markets globally.

What’s driving this change
Several things are happening simultaneously to enable this shift.
First, dealers are getting better at managing risk electronically. Over the past five years, banks have materially improved their ability to recycle risk across algorithmic trading, portfolio trading, ETF hedging and interdealer channels (including our own all-to-all Open Trading® network). Electronic liquidity providers have expanded coverage, particularly in index-linked instruments where ETF pricing creates strong correlation across underlying bonds. When risk moves through the system more efficiently, larger trades naturally become more feasible to execute on screen.
Second, there has been a generational shift in behavior. A growing proportion of traders treat electronic workflows as the default, not the exception. Request-for-quotes (RFQs), algorithmic pricing, and data-driven counterparty selection are simply how they operate. That familiarity reduces friction and, over time, changes institutional habits.
But the deeper changes are in the information environment around the trade. A decade ago, the decision about whether to trade a block electronically was largely a function of size. If the trade was big enough, it went to voice. Today, the decision is a function of how much you know: how confident you are in the pricing, how well you understand the counterparty landscape, and how clearly you can assess execution risk.
Access to liquidity and data are what is now important.
Liquidity and the protocol question
One of the most common misconceptions about block electronification is that it converges on a single protocol. It does not. In practice, clients are dynamically choosing between multiple protocols depending on size, urgency and market conditions.
In emerging markets, for example, request-for-market for competitive, two-way pricing has become a critical on-ramp for trading larger sizes electronically, precisely because liquidity is regionally fragmented, episodic, and dealer balance sheet matters.
In US credit, Targeted RFQ (TRFQ) and dealer risk recycling protocols are scaling rapidly. Targeted RFQ, designed for trade sizes of more than $3 million, solves the dealer selection pain point by suggesting up to eight sell-side players that are axed or have recently been active in the relevant bond, allowing the trader to accurately define his or her selection. Our clients go on to invite 80% of TRFQ-recommended dealers onto their tickets. Mid-X, our protocol for anonymous mid-point matching sessions, uses advanced risk controls that limit exposure to ensure users are not left with skewed risk positions post-session. Mid-X ADV grew 168% year-on-year in Q1.
A variety of protocols allows the trader to select the right protocol for the right trade in the right conditions.
The data flywheel
Every electronic block trade generates data. Even if full transparency is not mandated (e.g. TRACE block masking) or desirable, aggregated market data can feed back into pricing models, execution analysis, counterparty and protocol selection tools. More electronic trading produces better data, which produces better execution.
At MarketAxess, CP+™—our AI-powered pricing engine—sits at the centre of this loop. It incorporates not just executed trades but the full set of RFQ interactions on the platform, including responses that do not result in a trade, giving our clients a significantly richer view of liquidity than execution data alone.
AI as interpretation, not speed
There is enormous excitement about AI in fixed income trading right now. The work we are doing to embed gen-AI and agentic features into our products and platforms is further enhancing the information environment around a trade, which will undoubtedly increase the market’s comfortability in trading blocks. AI Select is a good example of this. It uses a broad set of historical trading metrics—more than thirty in total—to identify the most suitable dealer for a given inquiry. These include win rates, responsiveness, and execution outcomes, all of which are continuously recalibrated throughout the trading day. In backtesting, it has shown strong predictive capability in identifying top-performing counterparties.
Where this goes
The direction is clear. The confidence to trade blocks electronically will continue to rise due to better information, better tools, and better risk infrastructure. Multiple protocols will continue to coexist, and the sophistication of protocol selection will become a meaningful differentiator. Data quality and coverage will matter most, and AI will add a deeper layer of insight and interpretation to electronic block trading.

title: The market is adapting: what six months of transparency reform reveal about how bonds trade
text:
The market is adapting: what six months of transparency reform reveal about how bonds trade
In the last year, the UK Financial Conduct Authority ("FCA") and the European Securities and Markets Authority ("ESMA") introduced their new post-trade transparency regimes. As we set out in our previous article, the reforms widened the scope and sped up the timing of post-trade disclosure.
Six months on from the last of these changes, the data suggests that the market has accepted the new rules and is actively trading around them. Volumes are up, and tickets are getting bigger. Activity is moving towards more liquid assets, and we can see some corners of the market lining up to just above the deferral thresholds allowing for delayed publication.
To measure these changes consistently, this analysis compares 2025 and 2026 levels using the TraX® data universe, covering approximately 85% of the European and UK fixed income market. TraX Tape also ingests the FCA’s consolidated tape; although the feed is not included here, to keep the year-on-year comparison like-for-like.
Volumes increased, with the UK market reluctant at first
TraX data shows trading volumes rising in the six months after each regime went live. But the UK market saw some reluctance at first.
Under the FCA regime, activity was subdued for the first two months before moving above year-earlier levels. When ESMA’s regime followed three months later, we didn’t see this same dip. The volumes rose straight away.
One read of this is that the UK acted as the market's test run. By the time the ESMA rules had arrived, market participants had already seen how greater transparency played out in practice. This pattern is consistent with feedback from our clients that the market is getting more comfortable with the new regime.
Widened conditions may have also influenced activity. With heightened geopolitical volatility, the increase cannot be solely attributed to the transparency regimes alone.
Markers outside of the new regimes help to separate these effects. TraX data covering regions such as APAC and the US showed lower volumes and reduced volatility over the same period. These markets aren’t directly comparable, but they are a reasonable proxy for how the markets would trade without the introduction of transparency rules. The divergence suggests that trading activity in the FCA and ESMA jurisdictions was comparatively stronger than in the rest of the world under broadly similar macroeconomic conditions.

YoY change in monthly trading volume (2026 vs. 2025)

The x-axis shows months since the regime change. The y-axis shows the year-on-year change in monthly trading volume (2026 vs 2025), split by regime. Source: MarketAxess TraX.

Bigger tickets, later prints
The key question surrounding the new transparency regimes has been whether participants would adjust the size of their trades to take advantage of deferrals.
Under the new legislation, trades above set thresholds are subject to delayed publication, due to sensitivities surrounding trade size or instrument liquidity. For a dealer, this matters. Immediate publication can tell the market that a firm has taken a significant position before it has had a chance to hedge or offload risk.
With this incentive in mind, the market behaved as expected. A participant that might have traded £900,000 of a high-yield corporate bond in London could instead trade £1.1 million and qualify for a one-day deferral rather than real-time publication.
TraX data shows the trade-size distribution under the FCA regime moving towards larger buckets. The effect is strongest at the larger bucket sizes, where deferral periods are longest and the benefit of staying out of view is greatest.
FCA | YoY change in trade count by trade size bucket, trades above GBP 500k (2026 vs 2025)
The x-axis shows trade-size buckets in GBP (trades above £500k), aligned to the FCA transparency intervals. The y-axis shows the year-on-year change in trade count in each bucket under the FCA regime. Source: MarketAxess TraX.

A move towards liquid assets
The growth in volume was driven primarily by trading in governments. Corporate high yield saw consistent declines, and corporate investment grade fell to a lesser extent. The same pattern appeared under both regimes.
Part of this pattern is the flight to quality during an uncertain macro backdrop. However, it may also be linked to transparency. In highly liquid securities, one published trade tells the market relatively little, so greater visibility makes transparency less sensitive.

FCA | YoY change in monthly trading volume (2026 vs 2025)

ESMA | YoY change in monthly trading volume (2026 vs 2025)
The x-axis shows months since the regime change. The y-axis shows the year-on-year change in monthly trading volume (2026 vs 2025), split by asset type, for the FCA and ESMA regimes. Source: MarketAxess TraX.

UK linkers: the £5m line
UK inflation-linked gilts, or linkers, stand out as an example of the drift towards larger government tickets.
Linkers are more sensitive to trading conditions than traditional gilts, and the FCA regime includes specific provisions for them, including a £5 million deferral threshold. TraX data shows the share of linker trades between £2 million and £5 million falling in 2026, whilst the share above £5 million rose. There was little change at the lowest (£1 million to £2 million) and highest (£10 million and above) ends of this range.
The main movement occurred in the range just below the threshold, exactly where you’d expect if participants were sizing trades to clear the line. Transparency thresholds appear to be shaping behaviour.

FCA UK Linker trade-size distribution
The x-axis shows trade-size buckets in GBP around the FCA transparency thresholds, including the £5 million threshold for inflation-linked gilts. The y-axis shows each bucket's share of total trade count, 2025 vs 2026. Source: MarketAxess TraX.

Who is behind the trades?
Public regulatory data doesn’t answer the question of who is behind the changes. TraX allows this through giving direction and counterparty insights, alongside a cleansed regulatory feed.
This view has shown a clear split. The buy-side increased its market share of volume in both corporate investment grade and high yield, while banks and dealers moved the other way. Interdealer brokers shifted away from investment grade and towards high yield.
The chart shows the percentage-point change in share of traded volume (2026 vs 2025) by counterparty role, for corporate high yield and corporate investment grade. Source: MarketAxess TraX.

Turning transparency data into market insight
The transparency reforms have created more information about bond market activity. However, in order to generate meaningful insights, the data needs to be a clean, consolidated view with direction and context attached.
That’s what TraX Tape provides. Clients see the regulatory post-trade feed cleansed and normalised, next to TraX insight on direction and counterparty type that public data doesn’t capture.
We expect more change ahead, as participants continue to adjust to increased visibility. Behaviour around thresholds is likely to become more pronounced. The planned go-live of the ESMA bond consolidation tape in Q1 of 2027 should be another catalyst. TraX Tape will continue to bring these new datasets into a single source of decision-grade data giving clients visibility on how the market is adapting as it happens.

title: The rise of European credit automation
text:
The rise of European credit automation

Automation in European credit trading is moving from early adoption to mainstream execution. Greater transparency, deeper liquidity pools and the rapid expansion of high-quality data are reshaping how participants interact with the market. This evolution is being driven from both sides of the market. Buy side firms are increasingly automating liquidity-taking workflows to manage growing order volumes efficiently. At the same time, dealers are enhancing algorithmic pricing models, expanding coverage and increasing quote sizes. Together, these developments are improving execution quality and creating a demand for automation across the European credit market.
Client automation moves into the mainstream
Since launching our automation protocol, Auto-X™ RFQ in 2018, adoption has steadily accelerated, along with the way clients are using it. Among our largest clients in Q1 2026, approximately a third of tickets and 17% of Euro investment-grade volume were executed via Auto-X.
Buy side clients: increasingly customized and prescriptive

In Q1 2026, 75% of tickets and 52% of volume in sizes up to €5 million were automated by our largest automation clients. In the €3–€5 million EUR IG bucket, automation penetration across our client base increased significantly between Q1 2023 and Q1 2026, rising from 2% to 7% of both ticket count and traded volume. This 250% increase in automation share illustrates continued strong adoption.
Market-wide data from TraX® underscores the opportunity for automation in the market.
Automation: greater efficiency for EUR IG “non-blocks”1
1Yearly volume in “non-blocks” has increased by 43% between 2020 and 2025 according to TraX.

The data indicates that 97% of overall tickets in European credit were less than or equal to €5 million. Automating a greater number of those more liquid orders would offer desks the ability to reallocate time and expertise toward larger, more complex trades that benefit most from manual intervention.
Customization drives surge in automation
Clients want to improve efficiency, lower execution costs, and create more opportunities for price improvement. Auto-X RFQ delivers in all three areas. As an intuitive, rules-based automation tool, it allows clients to streamline part—or all—of their execution workflow while maintaining control over how trades are handled.
The benefits are twofold. First, Auto-X RFQ brings advanced, data-driven decision-making to the forefront. It is powered by CP+™, an AI-driven pricing engine for global credit and rates markets. By combining data from the MarketAxess network with public TRACE information and proprietary TraX inputs, CP+ enhances price discovery, transaction cost analysis, and algorithmic strategy development. This is further supported by the Relative Liquidity Score, which offers a clear view of a bond’s tradability and market depth. Tradability, our machine learning-based AI model, can be used as an expansion to that to predict market depth on a bond, side, and size level.
Second, Auto-X RFQ uses a dynamic waterfall framework for rule configuration. Clients can define automation parameters using variables such as trade size, price thresholds, number of respondents, and more. Through parameter modeling, historical data can be leveraged to evaluate the potential impact of automation before deployment. This level of flexibility supports higher automation rates, improves efficiency in larger trades—including block-sized orders—and allows multiple custom rule sets to be applied across different markets. The result is a more sophisticated and scalable automation workflow.
Dealer algos grow in size and coverage
As clients expand their use of automated trading, dealers are also responding: 65% of Euro HG responses were from algos in 2025, and the average number of responses per RFQ increased from 5.4 in 2023 to 7.1 in 2025. Dealer algos are also covering a broader share of the market: algo coverage expanded from 5,200 ISINs in 2023 to over 6,200 ISINs in 2025.
Top EU HG Dealer algo coverage2

2These areas represent the general coverage where the top dealers reside, by time period.

Crucially, algos are penetrating larger ticket sizes. In the €3–5 million range — once considered challenging for automation — algos accounted for 22% of responses in 2025, more than double the 10% seen in 2023.
As dealers increasingly price larger trades electronically, buy-side clients benefit from deeper liquidity and improved execution outcomes.

The MarketAxess advantage
MarketAxess continues to drive innovation in automation with Adaptive Auto-X, our latest automation protocol, which is currently being piloted in Europe following a successful rollout in the US. Adaptive Auto-X takes automation to new levels of precision and efficiency by dynamically adjusting execution criteria and execution channels to optimize trading outcomes. It uses smart order routing to integrate matching, responding, posting, and requesting across multiple execution protocols and liquidity pools.
This creates customized workflows aligned with specific trading objectives, all connected through Open Trading, our global, all-to-all, electronic marketplace. Combined with a dedicated global automation team, clients receive hands-on support to refine workflows and identify efficiency gains.
From expansion to expectation
Automation in European credit trading is no longer experimental, it’s becoming the norm. As both buy-side and sell-side participants expand capabilities, liquidity improves, execution becomes faster, and workflows grow more efficient.
With continued advances in data, transparency and AI-driven optimization, the frontier of European credit automation is not just expanding, it is becoming the new standard.

title: History in the making: A closer look at MarketAxess’ newly launched Opening and Closing Auctions
text:
History in the making: A closer look at MarketAxess’ newly launched Opening and Closing Auctions
MarketAxess’ new ‘Opening and Closing Auctions’ – a first for the fixed income market – is aimed at improving price discovery and providing access to unique liquidity for trading US credit through a standardised market-wide auction protocol.
With the launch having occurred in November, The TRADE decided to take a closer look at the new offering, delving into both the strategy itself and the potential for real market structure change as a result.

Liquidity paramount

The protocol combines real-time pricing and auction matching expertise from Pragma, an algorithmic trading solutions provider acquired by MarketAxess in 2023, resulting in a liquid end of day event, focused on hedging efficiency and solving inefficiencies in bond pricing.
Speaking to The TRADE, Kat Sweeney, global head of data and ETF solutions for MarketAxess, asserts that the new protocol addresses a “major market gap”, with the long-term vision being for the auction to become dominant in end of day credit trading.
“This is a way for asset managers, hedge funds, dealers to have a central point – same time, same place, same bonds – knowing when and how they can find liquidity.”   
This, of course, requires industry buy-in – something at the fore of the firm’s planning, with a collaborative design having been developed with the market in order to ensure efficacy and compliance. 
This has been key to the development of the auction protocol, with crucial input from the buy-side and sell-side over the past three years. These discussions span all corners of the industry and have shaped the protocol design to align with market needs.
MarketAxess’ advisory group includes names such as: BlackRock, DWS, State Street Investment Management, and AllianceBernstein.
“As the US Credit market grows, it is vital that participants innovate and deliver new liquidity solutions to investors. The auction protocol represents a step forward in advancing market structure and puts the public bond market on its front-foot in competing with other capital markets,” George Catrambone, head of fixed Income Americas at DWS Group, tells The TRADE.

Speaking to how the offering is set to impact fixed income markets, Sweeney highlights how equities activity shaped plans for the fixed income sphere.

“We have seen this before in the equity markets – the growth of indexation and ETFs coupled with the growth of systematic market makers saw a move on trading towards the close. Now the closing auction in equities is about 10% of total trading volume [and] the auction plays an important role for both the buy- and sell-side of the market.  
“In credit, we are facing the same backdrop just at an earlier stage in the cycle. ETFs and credit futures are becoming a larger part of the market, and we are seeing more systematic liquidity provision from the traditional dealers and market making community.”
The protocol integrates diverse liquidity sources, aligning with client trading patterns and improving benchmark tracking, however when it comes to the markets’ biggest concern, Sweeney confirms that completion is front of mind.
“We have to make sure the auction is a liquid event […] Benchmarks are changing and more trading is going toward the close. Traders are keeping flow open later because that’s where they benchmark.  
“If traders have a high degree of confidence on completion and knowing where end of day values will be set, they are willing to make larger markets across ETFs, cash credit and futures. I call this the bands of arbitrage.”

Looking ahead

Delving further, Sweeney explains that there is a wealth of benefits which could come from addressing what the credit market lacks – a universal closing price for the cash bonds that would then be used for all macro products, like ETFs and futures.
“The data from a closing auction can be used by end of day evaluators, like S&P Global, to set the end of day price or be a significant input into setting the price. That would be so powerful and would improve the overall market liquidity.”  
She further adds: “This can be used as a price for internal crossing […] every single asset manager brought it up without me even prompting them.”  
Speaking about the launch of this new auction protocol recently, Daniel Veiner, head of markets at BlackRock, affirmed that the offering “represents a meaningful advancement in the modernisation of the bond market.”  
He added: “These auctions will improve price discovery and offer investors increased transparency in-line with the continued growth of electronic trading. As fixed income markets continue to evolve, we’re committed to supporting solutions that better serve investors.”  
Addressing the industry on the MarketAxess earnings call in November 2025, Chris Concannon, chief executive, emphasised that the most important aspect of the strategy around the auction protocol is to support the growing indexation of the fixed income market – and is subsequently the key talking point with the firm’s client partners. 
“In US investment grade volumes, the last hour of the last day of the month, 25% of that day’s volume is done in that last hour. So, we’re seeing aggregation of activity moving to closer to the close.
“On a normal trading day, we’re now seeing almost 15% of total volume within the last hour of the close as well. There’s been a clear trend line where much of the bond market is moving closer and closer to the closing time of the day.”
Looking toward the future, Sweeney concludes that as more and more systematic credit comes to market, the players in this sphere are set to appreciate an auction – equal footing for all. 
“Within the next couple of years, this could be the dominant protocol in the market. We want to make this not just a protocol on our platform, but something that’s market-structure changing, and the wheels are already in motion. It can start slow, but we’re now in the beginning of the snowball phase.”
Offered at the beginning and end of the trading day, the protocol specifically relates to US high-grade and high-yield bonds on MarketAxess’s X-Pro trading platform.

title: Electronic bond trading expanding to match MENA markets rapid growth
text:
Electronic bond trading expanding to match MENA markets rapid growth
Bond markets in the Middle East & North Africa (MENA) region have seen primary and secondary activity surging in 2025, reflecting individual country’s sovereign strengths, regional corporate expansion, and greater international investor appetite, positioning the region as a growing hub for global fixed-income investors.
Bond issuance across the broader Middle East and Africa regions as tracked by Dealogic has hit a record US$223 billion in 2025 year-to-date. This marks a 30% year-on-year increase across sovereign and corporate bond issuers, who are tapping global capital markets to diversify their funding sources amid shifting local- and macro-economic conditions.
Of that, Sovereign, Supranational and Agency (SSA) constitutes US$122 billion, investment grade (IG) US$82 billion and high yield (HY) US$16.5 billion.
Within the Middle East specifically, the London Stock Exchange Group reported issuance of US$125.9 by September, with Saudi Arabia offering US$67.6 billion of bonds and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) placing the second largest offerings of $32.7 billion. Israel issued US$27 billion of fixed rate bonds and US$13 billion of CPI linked bonds.
“We expect publicly listed corporates’ annual capex needs will reach about $85 billion-$95 billion over 2025-2027, translating into an increase in corporate lending demand and cross-border issuance,” S&P Global analysts noted in in a paper in mid-November.
The higher levels of primary market activity supported liquidity in the secondary markets as well.
MarketAxess has seen MENA credit volumes increase by 7% overall in 2025, with a 23% increase in MENA corporate volumes.
“When we look at the breakdown of clients who are trading the sector, we see 70% of all volume being traded by Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) based clients and 26% from North American clients,” Dan Burke, global head of emerging markets
“Volumes are relatively even between e-trading and voice enquiries, but clearly the voice enquiries can be extremely large, particularly when the larger local accounts are involved,” noted one Tier 1 dealer.
Although smaller trades are more commonly executed electronically, block trades are also being increasingly facilitated by electronic protocols. These allow dealers to support direct execution with specific clients, while managing larger rebalances using portfolio trades and all-to-all trading to reduce information leakage.
“Electronic trading of MENA sovereign blocks for US$5 million or greater increased 9% this year,” says Burke. “When we look at the universe of MENA trades on the platform this year, trades using our all-to-all trading protocol Open Trading made up 47% of total MENA volume, an increase of 23% year over year.”
This growth is likely to increase as global investors are explicitly sought out by local issuers to support their financing.
Market confidence had been weakened by the threat of expanding regional conflicts and wildly unpredictable US trade policies, but nevertheless investor appetite remained strong this year, supported by oil revenues, sovereign surpluses, and rating upgrades in countries like Oman, Morocco and Tunisia.
Confidence also rose in Egypt as it returned to the international debt markets, successfully drawing in Gulf State foreign direct investment (FDI), including an US$18.5 billion deal to support tourism from Saudi Arabian and Emirati investors.
The S&P analysts noted, “Large Saudi corporates are strategically diversifying their funding base by reaching out to global investors, while extending their maturity profiles. We view these developments as credit supportive but will monitor whether the accumulation of debt from these investments outpaces earnings generation.”

title: MarketAxess expands Mid-X protocol
text:
MarketAxess expands Mid-X protocol
MarketAxess has successfully launched an enhanced Mid-X protocol this past year, expanding its anonymous mid-point matching session, rolling it out for emerging markets and Eurobonds, and, more recently, for US Credit. As it is fast becoming a preferred market protocol with dealers, Steve Tait, Head of US Dealer Execution Business at MarketAxess explains what’s behind its growing success and what’s on the horizon for Mid-X and MarketAxess dealer solutions.
Mid-X offers a unique protocol for dealer-to-dealer matching. How does it work?
Mid-X streamlines interdealer matching with a one-step process that’s faster and more efficient than traditional approaches.
The predominant protocol has been a two-step process: dealers first load their interest and wait for the system to indicate offsetting interest, then return to the platform where a mid-price is set, and they decide whether to attempt to match.
Mid-X eliminates that back-and-forth waiting period. Users enter the platform, immediately see a mid-price, decide whether to submit to match, and MarketAxess matches at the end of the Submit window. A dealer could complete the entire process in under a minute if needed.
One of the other benefits of Mid-X is an extremely reliable mid-level price. Mid-X is powered by CP+™, our award-winning, predictive pricing engine. Our CP+ mid-price is derived from real tradable levels, including US TRACE, TraX®, and RFQ inventory data — calibrated independently and objectively. It’s not just your average indicative mid-price, but one of the most accurate and reliable mid-pricing tools available in the market.
Beyond speed and pricing, what other advantages does Mid-X offer?
In addition to providing a true, best mid-price, our one-step process using CP+ stops information leakage by preventing participants from loading interest and then pulling it when they see offsetting interest.
So, participants can join daily, anonymous, mid-point matching sessions using unbiased CP+ pricing levels. Our no-name give-up protocol reveals only the matched size, so dealers can confidently tap into a vast pool of liquidity without information leakage concerns. Dealers who do not commit firm risk do not get any color.
Finally, Mid-X also minimizes risk — we’ve built in advanced risk controls that limit exposure to ensure users are not left with skewed risk positions post-session. Dealers can confidently submit large numbers of orders across multiple sectors and maturity buckets.
Since relaunching Mid-X in the US, you’ve had a record month in September and a record quarter in Q3. Tell us more about the rollout and global adoption of the platform.
Adoption has been strong and steady. We’re now live in the US, Europe, APAC, and CEEMEA. Outside of the US, we’ve doubled volumes YoY from 2024, and in the US, we have exceeded 2bn printed. This year, we’ve launched Asia, CEEMEA, and Swiss Mid-X sessions, and are running up to 6 times a day, with over 60 unique dealer firms having accessed the protocol.
Dealers were looking for a different approach for mid-point matching — one that delivers shorter, faster sessions with precision pricing, no information leakage, and reduced risk. Mid-X provides dealers with easier access to liquidity, increased workflow efficiency, and a better tool to recycle risk.
What’s next for Mid-X?
We’re focused on two priorities: product enhancements and global expansion.
On the technology side, we’re integrating Pragma technology as the backbone of our entire system and the foundation for the MarketAxess platform. This will enhance trading efficiency and deliver better execution quality. We are also upgrading the Mid-X user interface to X-Pro for enhanced workflows and customizable features. We will add API connectivity, which will allow algos and tech-savvy dealers to interact with our sessions. LATAM would be a natural next region of expansion, given we already have local presence via our LiveMarkets and LiveMarkets Match.
How does MarketAxess support dealers using Mid-X?
Mid-X is backed by our DealerAxess team, a dedicated ‘white-glove’ service to line traders to bring more liquidity to the platform and facilitate trading. It’s a global team of market specialists with decades of combined experience in trading, sales, broking, on-desk operations, and settlements. They provide comprehensive, high-touch support throughout the trading journey, from pre- to post-trade. The team gives dealers real-time feedback at the point of trade, keeping them connected throughout the trade process. As a result, dealers can confidently partner with the DealerAxess team to leverage a significantly larger network that spans multiple regions and jurisdictions, scaling their business to levels previously out of reach.
You spent more than 25 years at JPMorgan, in several senior roles in global credit trading and electronic trading, most recently as executive director of global credit trading, overseeing systematic market making and algorithmic trading. Now at MarketAxess, you’re developing liquidity solutions for dealers in credit markets. What has been the biggest change you’ve seen in your career, and where do you see the market heading?
The biggest change I’ve seen in my career has taken place in just the last five years, during which time we have seen an explosion of algorithmic trading and desks thinking about risk holistically. Dealers are implementing a more centralized approach to risk across trading desks and a more algorithmic, e-friendly approach to making markets.
Pre-trade data quality and transparency is certainly increasing on both buy and sell side desks. The ability and willingness to stream and participate in electronic protocols is growing. Many of the major broker-dealers now have algos which price suggest, trade autonomously, and manage their own risk. Session trading is benefiting from these developments and is becoming increasingly automated and low-touch.
As we move towards greater automation and more dealer participation, there could potentially be a world with continuous mid-point matching.
What’s next for you at MarketAxess?
I’m excited to be at MarketAxess, leading the charge for our dealer solutions, focused on developing products that will help dealers connect to clients, manage their risk, and generate profits in the credit markets. Mid-X is one part of that puzzle, but there’s more to come. We have another new product launching called Targeted Axes that I’m really enthused about. It’s another dealer-friendly solution that will help dealers trade more efficiently with their clients, with even more functionality. It will allow dealers to engage their clients with their firm, block axes, and manage the disclosed trade through to booking.
MarketAxess CEO Chris Concannon has articulated a strategic focus on the dealer-initiated channel. How does Mid-X fit within that vision, and how is MarketAxess positioned to drive continued innovation and success for dealers?
Mid-X is one in a portfolio of tools focused on enhancing dealer value. Within our dealer solutions ecosystem, dealers have continuous access to liquidity throughout the day in multiple ways; dealer-to-dealer via Mid-X, via Open Trading® with Dealer RFQ, Live Markets or Match, and soon, disclosed with their clients through Targeted Axes.
With our strong history in Open Trading, the broadest range of liquidity options, our leadership position in the market, and our unmatched network, we’re uniquely positioned to lead the market into the future of electronification.

title: Milei’s victory saw Argentinian debt traders reach for rapid risk transfer
text:
Milei’s victory saw Argentinian debt traders reach for rapid risk transfer
In late October 2025, Argentine President Javier Milei’s party, La Libertad Avanza, scored a decisive win, in the country’s midterm elections, a political triumph that significantly strengthens his mandate and numbers in congress to implement radical economic reforms. The win, particularly in the historically Peronist stronghold of Buenos Aires province, surprised many observers after earlier election in Buenos Aires had suggested his support was faltering, the outcome potentially marks a turning point in Argentina’s political and fiscal trajectory.
For traders, this surprise was measurable in the substantially increased use of block trades, that allowed rapid transfer of risk for large positions, and of all-to-all electronic trading, both of which reduce the market impact of orders, and accelerate order matching speeds. 
Argentina Daily Trade Volume and Count October 2025
On Monday 27 October after the weekend election, dollar-denominated government bond prices jumped. Analysts at Morgan Stanley noted that Argentinian debt resulted in swings in fund alpha, with overweight positions paying off in the week after the election. Trading volumes spiked but trade sizes did not, indicating that trading was conducted at speed across large and small orders. 
Inconclusive value picture
“Argentina's YTD performance has reached 10.1%, 18.8% returns just this past week,” wrote Simon Weaver, Emma Cerda, Neville, Mamdimika and Guru Sharan Agrawal, all strategists at the bank. “While strong, this is still below the 13.2% YTD index returns, meaning OW positions have not yet paid off this year.”
In October, average daily volume (ADV) of Argentinian bonds on MarketAxess hit US$307 million, an increase of 41% year-to-date ADV of US$217 million.
“Funds likely went into the elections this weekend with less risk on,” noted the Morgan Stanley strategists in an 30 October note. “Looking at our EPFR data with a smaller sample of funds, we find that just in September, funds reduced exposure to the name by 0.36 percentage points (pps) to bring exposure closer to flat, below historical averages. While October data are not available, this suggests that funds went into the recent elections with less exposure to the credit. That said, just on Monday [27 October], funds gained 12bp in fund alpha on aggregate, increasing MTD alpha to -5bp. If only driven by Argentina, this would suggest that funds were able to benefit from the move, although not by enough to turn MTD alpha positive.”
However, Argentina's YTD performance has reached 10.1%, which is below the 13.2% YTD index returns, they observed, meaning OW positions would not yet have paid off this year.
The US Treasury has extended a US$20 billion FX swap line and has reportedly bought Argentinian pesos at several points over the past month.
This emphasises the need for investors to deliver effective trading of their positions in order to minimise trading costs. On the MarketAxess platform, October saw the ADV of block trades – meaning orders over US$5 million in value – hit US$40 million, where year-to-date block trading ADV had been US$28 million. 
Its Open Trading protocol saw ADV of US$255 million in October, also a substantial increase on YTD ADV of US$176 million.
Investors look ahead
The midterm results now give Milei’s Liberty Advances party greater legislative leverage to push through sweeping reforms in labour, taxation, and public sector restructuring. This consolidation of power will be crucial for implementing his vision of a leaner state and a free-market economy.
Yet despite his rhetoric of fiscal discipline, Milei’s government had paradoxically increased spending in areas such as pensions, health, and education in the lead-up to the midterms. This move, seen by some as political pragmatism, also raised questions about the sustainability of his zero-deficit pledge. While his administration has made strides in reducing inflation and narrowing the gap between official and parallel exchange rates, the durability of these gains depends on maintaining investor confidence and access to external financing.
Milei’s approach to government borrowing is shaped by his deep scepticism of debt-fuelled public spending. However, Argentina’s economic reality – marked by a history of defaults, inflation, and capital flight – necessitates engagement with international lenders.
Judging Argentinian investment in 2026 
Since taking office, Milei has negotiated new arrangements with the International Monetary Fund (IMF), securing continued disbursements in exchange for structural reforms. While this has helped stabilise Argentina’s macroeconomic outlook in the short term, it also deepens the country’s dependence on external creditors.
On one hand, a credible commitment to fiscal discipline could lower borrowing costs and restore access to capital markets. On the other, the reliance on IMF support and the social toll of austerity may undermine long-term stability.
Milei’s success will be judged not just by his ability to cut deficits, but by whether he can do so while preserving social cohesion and economic growth. As seen by returns to date, emerging market investors will need to be well compensated for the risks taken in investing in Argentinian debt over alternatives. The next year will be critical in determining whether Argentina can finally break free from its cycle of debt and dysfunction.

title: MarketAxess Unveils Fixed Income's First Opening & Closing Auctions; Designed to Improve Pricing and Liquidity
text:
Market-focused solution built in consultation with AllianceBernstein, BlackRock, DWS and State Street Investment Management

NEW YORK--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- MarketAxess Holdings Inc. (Nasdaq: MKTX), the operator of a leading electronic trading platform for fixed income securities, today announced the upcoming launch of Opening and Closing Auctions—the first standardized market-wide auction protocol designed to improve price discovery and provide access to unique liquidity for trading U.S. credit.
In developing the new Opening & Closing Auctions, MarketAxess consulted a diverse group of buy-side and sell-side participants to advise and help design the auction trading protocol. Advisory group members include AllianceBernstein, BlackRock, DWS, and State Street Investment Management.
“Today’s fixed income markets are evolving quickly and there is a clear need for a market-wide auction protocol where price can be formed and liquidity can be unlocked,” said Kat Sweeney, Global Head of Data & ETF Solutions at MarketAxess. “Auctions in derivatives and equity markets have proven to reduce volatility, increase transparency and concentrate liquidity.”
“MarketAxess has always believed in building not just for today’s markets, but for the markets of the future. With the growth of fixed income ETFs, credit derivatives, and portfolio trading, the fixed income market’s needs are rapidly changing. We felt it was important to build a protocol to support price formation and liquidity at the most critical times of the day,” said Chris Concannon, Chief Executive Officer of MarketAxess. “I would like to thank our partners at AllianceBernstein, BlackRock, DWS and State Street for the instrumental role they have played in the development, testing, and support of the Opening and Closing Auctions protocol.”
The new auction protocol will be available to clients and dealers in the coming weeks and will be offered at the beginning and end of the trading day for U.S. high-grade and high-yield bonds on MarketAxess’s X-Pro Trading platform. For more information on the Opening and Closing Auctions, please visit: www.marketaxess.com/trade/auctions

title: Corporate bond world set to get first daily Closing Auction
text:
Corporate bond world set to get first daily Closing Auction
MarketAxess Holdings Inc. is seeking to bring a feature of fast-twitch equity markets to the relatively sedate $9 trillion universe of corporate bonds: the daily closing auction.
The electronic trading company plans to launch a daily “closing print” for corporate bonds — the first standardized end-of-day price in a market long defined by opaque, ad hoc quotes. The goal is to deepen liquidity and lower trading costs, but the worry is there’s a tradeoff if it squeezes dealer profits tied to the very inefficiencies it would eliminate.
“There are lots of matching sessions in the fixed-income market today,” Chris Concannon, the firm’s chief executive officer, said in an interview. “There’s no tradeable true auctions. This is the first.”
The closing-auction process — supported by industry titans including BlackRock Inc., State Street Investment Management, AllianceBernstein Holding LP and DWS Group — will match buy and sell interests from dealers and investors to find a single closing price of a bond, according to Concannon.
The auction system will be available to clients and dealers in the coming weeks and will initially be available to a select list of highly liquid bonds, including those within major exchange-traded funds and recently issued bonds, he added. MarketAxess also plans to roll out an opening auction.
The change to the trading process comes amid rapid structural shifts in the bond market, as traders embrace portfolio trading, fixed-income ETFs and adopt electronic, high-speed strategies — innovations familiar to equity markets.
In stocks, major exchanges like the New York Stock Exchange use a daily closing auction to consolidate liquidity and determine an official end-of-day price, providing a reference point for indexes, funds and derivatives.
Credit markets, by contrast, have long operated through fragmented and bilateral negotiations with little visibility into where bonds actually trade. The new closing protocol seeks to change that.
More price transparency widens the scope of data available for systematic investors — who make fast decisions about corporate bonds to buy and sell using complicated algorithms — and expands their opportunity set, according to Andrew Dassori, chief investment officer at Wavelength Capital Management LLC.
“Growing liquidity at market close helps make these trades executable,” said Dassori.
The closing price will, over time, become a reference point for companies looking to sell bonds in the primary market, much like how new issues work in other markets, Concannon said.
While dealers long accustomed to the profits eked out from the inefficiencies brought about by traditional voice trading and request-for-quote processes may take an initial hit, Concannon views auctions as a new way to provide and profit from liquidity by offsetting multiple clients’ supply and demand imbalances. The auction format will allow dealers to also act as principals while capitalizing on price discrepancies that emerge during concentrated trading windows, he added.
“Dealers can exit inventory on an auction or they can be a liquidity provider in an auction,” Concannon said. “So it offers them another trading tool to both be a dealer or to exit inventory positions.”
It’s a major shift for a market that has for years relied on dealer runs — or a list of bond prices from dealers — and trades that occurred much earlier in the day rather than on actual closing transactions. That’s made it difficult to find the fair value when looking to buy or sell a bond.
“These auctions will improve price discovery and offer investors increased transparency in line with the continued growth of electronic trading,” said Daniel Veiner, head of markets within BlackRock global markets and index investing.

Still, success will depend on adoption because without deep participation from dealers and buy-side firms, auction volumes may remain limited, Concannon noted. Ahead, he sees a potential opportunity for a single, market-wide auction that brings together both dealers and buy-side participants to establish a unified close for fixed-income trading that could potentially expand across asset classes.
“Auctions will ultimately grow into other areas of the fixed-income market, particularly the US Treasury market,” said Concannon.
Bloomberg LP, the parent company of Bloomberg News, competes with electronic platforms including MarketAxess and Tradeweb Markets Inc. to offer fixed-income trading, data and information to the financial services industry.
— With assistance from Sid Verma
